heroBody: The QLED TV market in the US is more competitive than it has ever been: Samsung no longer owns the value tier on its own, TCL and Hisense now ship genuinely good quantum-dot panels at aggressive price points, and the gap between a mid-range QLED and a flagship OLED has shrunk to a few hundred dollars in some screen sizes. The right pick depends on what you watch, how bright your room is, and whether you game or not. This page pulls live US listings from BuyWhere's catalog so you can see what Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, Costco and the direct-to-consumer brands are charging today, and matches that against the screen-size and panel-generation advice that actually matters.

highlightSectionTitle: What changed in QLED TVs this year

highlights.title: Quantum-dot is now standard, not premium
highlights.body: Two years ago, quantum-dot was a Samsung premium feature. In 2026, quantum-dot panels are standard across the QLED tier from Samsung, TCL and Hisense — even mid-range sets now hit a meaningful percentage of the DCI-P3 colour gamut, which matters for HDR movies and sports. If a 'QLED' listing does not list its colour-gamut coverage, treat it as a red flag.

highlights.title: Mini-LED has changed the value calculus
highlights.body: Mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming now reach the 55- and 65-inch tiers at mainstream QLED prices. The difference between a mid-tier QLED and a flagship OLED is narrower than it has ever been, especially in bright rooms where QLED's higher peak brightness actually matters more than OLED's perfect blacks.

highlights.title: Gaming features are now table stakes
highlights.body: 4K at 120 Hz, variable refresh rate (VRR), ALLM, and a low input lag are no longer flagship-only. Mid-range QLEDs that skip these features are now visibly worse for PS5 and Xbox Series X gaming. Check the spec sheet before you buy — particularly the HDMI 2.1 port count.

highlights.title: Smart-TV platforms have fragmented
highlights.body: Samsung uses Tizen, Hisense uses Google TV, TCL uses Google TV or Roku depending on the line, and Hisense and TCL both sell Fire TV editions. Pick the platform you already use on your phone or laptop — switching costs are higher than they look. The live US listings on this page show which platform each set runs.

adviceSectionTitle: How to buy the right QLED TV in the US
advicePoints: Buy the right screen size for the room, not the biggest you can afford. Sit about 1.2 to 1.6 times the screen diagonal away for 4K — a 65-inch set in a 10-foot room is right; the same set in an 8-foot room is overwhelming.

Prioritise peak brightness and local dimming over resolution. 4K is standard; what separates a good QLED from a great one is how bright it gets for HDR and how well it manages blooming in dark scenes. Spec sheets list peak brightness in nits — 700+ is good, 1000+ is great.

Check the HDMI 2.1 port count if you game. A TV with one HDMI 2.1 port and two HDMI 2.0 ports cannot run a current-gen console at 4K 120 Hz while a soundbar or AV receiver is plugged into the second port. Two HDMI 2.1 ports is the practical minimum; four is ideal.

Buy from a US retailer with a real return policy. A 65-inch QLED is too big to ship back casually; Amazon, Best Buy, Costco and Walmart all have free returns within a window that lets you live with the set for a couple of weeks before committing.

Time the buy around Super Bowl, March Madness and Black Friday. US TV prices drop meaningfully in late January and again in late November; if you can wait, the same set is often 20–35% cheaper than at launch.
Do not overpay for sound. Built-in TV speakers are an afterthought on every mainstream QLED; budget for a soundbar or a basic 2.1 system if you care about dialogue clarity and bass.
faqSectionTitle: QLED TVs in the US — common questions

faqs.question: Is QLED better than OLED for a bright US living room?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most bright living rooms QLED wins. QLED panels with mini-LED backlights get significantly brighter than OLED, which matters in rooms with lots of windows. OLED still wins in dark rooms for perfect blacks and pixel-level contrast. The live US listings on this page show the current pricing across both technologies.

faqs.question: Which QLED TV brand is best in the US?
faqs.answer: Samsung still makes the most-refined QLED panels, but TCL and Hisense now ship genuinely competitive quantum-dot sets at noticeably lower prices. For most buyers in 2026, the right brand is the one that has the right screen size and feature set at the right price on the day you buy — and that varies by week. The live listings help you compare on the day that matters.

faqs.question: When is the cheapest time to buy a QLED TV in the US?
faqs.answer: Two windows: late January through early March around the Super Bowl and March Madness, and late November around Black Friday. US TV prices also dip in late August as new model-year stock arrives. The live listings on this page show the current prices across the calendar.

faqs.question: Do I need HDMI 2.1 on a QLED TV?
faqs.answer: Yes if you game on PS5, Xbox Series X or a modern PC. HDMI 2.1 is what enables 4K at 120 Hz, variable refresh rate (VRR), and auto low-latency mode (ALLM). Without it, your console and PC can still run, but at lower frame rates or with screen tearing. Two HDMI 2.1 ports is the practical minimum.

faqs.question: Is a 75-inch QLED worth it over a 65-inch?
faqs.answer: Only if your seating distance is right. At 4K, the sweet-spot seating distance is 1.2 to 1.6 times the screen diagonal — so 75-inch in a 10- to 12-foot room, 65-inch in an 8- to 10-foot room. A 75-inch set in an 8-foot room is overwhelming and does not look better; a 65-inch in a 12-foot room feels small.

categoryIntro.heading: Why the US QLED TV market is unusually competitive in 2026
categoryIntro.body: The US TV market is dominated by four major brands — Samsung, LG, TCL and Hisense — and all four now ship quantum-dot QLED panels at meaningful price points, with Roku, Google TV, Tizen and Fire TV smart platforms creating real differentiation on top of the hardware. Mini-LED backlights, full-array local dimming and HDMI 2.1 are no longer flagship-only. This page tracks the listings that are actually available, at the prices they actually trade for, so you can pick the right QLED for your room and your wallet rather than chase the lowest sticker.
